key_claims: Leroy 2009 (from the RePEc abstract summary): across two experiments, people switching between tasks have trouble fully shifting attention. Leaving the earlier task unfinished makes the shift hard and hurts performance on the next task. Finishing a task is not enough by itself; time pressure on the prior task helped people disengage and improved next-task performance. Mark et al. 2008: interruptions, whether of the same or a different topic as the main task, made no difference to disruption cost; interrupted people finished the email task faster with no loss in quality but reported more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. Murty et al. 2022 (snippet only): app and website toggling is frequent and the authors argue the cost comes from how work and tools are designed. NOTE: all three are about knowledge work in general (email, project tasks, office apps), not about AI agents or agent sessions. Any link to juggling several agent sessions is the essay's inference, not something these sources test.
headline_figures: Mark et al.: 48 participants; 3 conditions, 12 emails per condition; interruptions every 2 minutes. Mean time to perform task (minutes, SD): baseline 22.77 (7.60), same-context interruption 20.31 (5.94), different-context 20.60 (4.93); B vs S and B vs D p<.05. Errors per email set: 1.94 vs 1.93 vs 1.84, not significant.

Mark et al. workload, NASA-TLX 1-20 scale (baseline / same / different): stress 6.92 / 9.46 / 9.13; frustration 4.73 / 6.63 / 6.48; effort 9.50 / 11.04 / 11.52; time pressure 11.02 / 12.69 / 12.17; mental workload 10.02 / 10.83 / 11.50. Stress and frustration differences p<.01 or better vs baseline.
Mark et al. personality: openness to experience and need for personal structure predicted time to complete interrupted work, R2 = .14 (small).

what_makes_oversight_tiring: Not about oversight. Leroy's mechanism is attention residue: thinking about the unfinished earlier task persists and competes with the new one, mainly when the earlier task is left incomplete. Mark et al.'s mechanism is compensation: people speed up to make up for lost time, which raises felt stress, frustration, pressure and effort. HBR authors blame fragmented tool and workflow design (snippet).
consequence_for_quality: Leroy: worse performance on the next task after switching away from an unfinished one (abstract-level). Mark et al.: no measurable drop in quality (errors, politeness unchanged) over a 12-email block; the cost showed up as stress and effort instead. The authors say they cannot tell whether people cope or the strain grows over longer periods. HBR: time lost (about 9% of time) per snippet, not quality.
what_reduces_the_load: Leroy (abstract-level): finishing the prior task, and time pressure on the prior task, helped people disengage. A later Leroy and Glomb 'ready-to-resume plan' (write down where you were and what comes next) is mentioned only in a secondary search summary and was not opened. [uncertain] Mark et al.: suggest systems that track and control interruptions over a long period so people are not overloaded; individual differences (openness, need for structure) matter. HBR: redesign of workflows and tool choice (snippet).
limitations_stated: Mark et al.: lab setting ("While laboratory studies are always subject to criticism of ecological validity"), mostly student sample, short 20-minute exposure, and "We cannot say whether people would cope over time or if these measures would only increase." They also note a possibility that interruptions do lengthen task time, but only right after the interruption, which they did not measure. Leroy and HBR limits not seen.
counter_evidence: Mark et al. itself cuts against a simple 'switching hurts output' story: interrupted work was faster with no quality loss; the cost was felt strain. Their interruptions were imposed by a supervisor and were not self-chosen switches, so they differ from a person deliberately cycling between agent sessions. Leroy's residue effect depends on leaving a task unfinished, so a clean hand-off point may avoid it. The HBR per-switch cost (about two seconds) is tiny and counts app changes, not deep task changes; it should not be equated with attention residue. None of the three studies involve AI agents.

usable_claim: Lab studies of knowledge work (not agents) find that moving on from an unfinished task leaves attention on it and hurts performance on the next task (Leroy 2009, abstract-level), and that being interrupted every couple of minutes made people work faster at the price of more stress, frustration and effort, with no quality drop over 12 emails (Mark et al. 2008, 48 students, lab). Applying this to several agent sessions is an inference.
do_not_use: The HBR numbers (1,200 switches a day, 9%, four hours a week, five weeks a year) until the article or the underlying Soroco data is opened. Any '23 minutes to refocus' style figure (not in these sources). The 588 billion dollars figure. Any claim that these studies show harm from running multiple agents, or that Leroy's work has been tested on software engineers. Any claim of a quality drop from Mark et al. (they found none).
